content: Insecticide-based strategies, such as long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS), are the primary methods for controlling malaria vectors. These approaches are designed to target mosquitoes that feed and rest indoors. However, they are less effective in preventing malaria transmission that occurs outdoors or outside of typical sleeping hours. In regions with low malaria endemicity, achieving malaria elimination will require addressing these gaps in control measures and identifying complementary tools. Topical repellents may be particularly beneficial for populations who are less likely to benefit from standard malaria control programs, such as refugees, military personnel, or individuals who spend time in forested areas. The objective of this Cochrane Review was to evaluate the effectiveness of topical repellents, either alone or in combination with other interventions (such as LLINs or IRS), in reducing the incidence of malaria among populations living in endemic areas, including both high-risk and non-high-risk groups. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was performed up to January 11, 2023. These databases included the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CAB Abstracts, and LILACS. Additional searches were conducted on trial registration platforms and conference proceedings, and relevant organizations and companies were contacted to identify ongoing or unpublished trials. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) that evaluated topical repellents proven to repel mosquitoes. Non-randomized studies were also included if they met specific inclusion criteria, such as controlled before-after studies, controlled interrupted time series, and controlled cross-over trials. Four authors independently assessed the trials for inclusion and extracted data, while two authors evaluated the risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Disagreements were resolved by a fifth author. Data were analyzed using meta-analysis, with results stratified by whether the study population was at high risk of malaria infection. Results from cRCTs and RCTs were combined after adjusting for clustering, and findings were presented using forest plots. The GRADE framework was used to assess the certainty of the evidence. Only data on Plasmodium falciparum infections were included in the meta-analysis. Thirteen articles corresponding to eight trials met the inclusion criteria and were qualitatively described. Six trials (five cRCTs and one RCT) were included in the meta-analysis. Effect on Malaria Incidence: Topical repellents may slightly reduce the combined incidence of P. falciparum infection and clinical malaria cases (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.56 to 0.98; 3 cRCTs and 1 RCT, 61,651 participants; low-certainty evidence). However, when these outcomes were analyzed separately, no significant effect was observed. Specifically, two cRCTs and one RCT (12,813 participants) assessed the effect of topical repellents on infection incidence (IRR 0.76, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.02; low-certainty evidence). One cRCT (48,838 participants) evaluated their effect on clinical case incidence (IRR 0.66, 95% CI 0.32 to 1.36; low-certainty evidence). Among the included studies, three (2 cRCTs and 1 RCT) involved high-risk populations, while one cRCT did not include high-risk participants. Adverse Events: Topical repellents were found to be safe, with a very low prevalence of adverse events (0.6%, 283/47,515 participants). Reported adverse events were limited to mild skin reactions. Effect on Malaria Prevalence: Topical repellents may slightly reduce the prevalence of P. falciparum (odds ratio [OR] 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.97; 3 cRCTs and 1 RCT; 55,366 participants; low-certainty evidence). Two of these studies (1 cRCT and 1 RCT) were conducted in refugee camps and exclusively included high-risk populations who were not receiving any other vector control interventions. Authors' Conclusions: There is insufficient evidence to definitively conclude that topical repellents can prevent malaria in settings where other vector control measures are in place. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was rated as low, primarily due to the risk of bias. However, a potential protective effect was observed among high-risk populations, particularly refugees, who may lack access to standard vector control measures. Additional well-powered clinical trials conducted in refugee camps could provide more robust evidence regarding the potential benefits of topical repellents in these settings. Individually randomized studies are also needed to determine whether topical repellents provide personal protection and to assess the extent to which diversion of mosquitoes to non-protected individuals influences overall transmission dynamics. Despite these findings, the potential additional benefits of topical repellents are likely to be limited in contexts where other effective interventions are already in place.
